bib.title: Branch-Solve-Merge Improves Large Language Model Evaluation and Generation

read.skipped: reference list skimmed for lineage only

question: Can a prompted decomposition into parallel sub-tasks (branch, solve, merge) improve LLM-as-judge correctness and consistency and constrained text generation over zero-shot, plan&solve and self-consistency?
hypothesis: Multi-faceted tasks fail because LLMs cannot plan or decompose; branching into parallel sub-problems, solving each independently and fusing them should improve correctness and reduce biases.
contributions: BRANCH-SOLVE-MERGE (BSM), an LLM program of branch, solve and merge modules, each a prompt to the same base LLM
Application to pairwise LLM response evaluation on MT-Bench, improving human agreement and reducing position and length bias
Application to constrained story generation (10 concepts), improving constraint satisfaction and coherence

method.summary: A fixed LLM program with three zero-shot prompts to one base LLM. Branch generates a plan of sub-problems (up to five evaluation criteria, or two concept groups plus a story topic), solve handles each branch independently, merge fuses results (sum of criterion scores for evaluation; an LLM fuse of two stories for generation). Evaluation runs twice with response order swapped and returns a tie if the two verdicts disagree.
method.task: pairwise LLM response evaluation (LLM-as-judge) and constrained story generation

datasets.name: MT-Bench
datasets.size: 2400 LLM responses and 3000 expert human judgements; 80 instructions from 8 domains, two turns each; 6 models give 15 response pairs, 300 pair samples per category
datasets.split: per category: writing (main), roleplay, extraction, reasoning, math, coding, STEM, humanities
datasets.preprocessing: reference-based categories (coding, reasoning, math) append a GPT-4 generated answer to the prompt; Table 7 uses a random subset of 100 samples; Tables 10 and 11 use 100 writing samples

datasets.name: Constrained story generation (CommonGen-Hard variant)
datasets.source: harder variant of CommonGen (Lin et al., 2020), concepts from Madaan et al., 2023 commongen_hard.jsonl

other.note: base LLM for BSM, evaluation only
base LLM for BSM in evaluation; also reference-answer generator and story-quality judge

inference.decoding: greedy decoding for all BSM modules; self-consistency baseline samples at temperature 0.7
inference.temperature: 0.7 for self-consistency and BSM+SC only; greedy otherwise
inference.samples: BSM: 1 solution per branch, 2 runs per item (original and swapped order). Self-consistency: same number of samples as the branching factor; majority vote per encoding order. BSM+SC: 5 evaluations per branch, averaged. Seeds not stated.
inference.prompting: zero-shot, module-specific instructions only, no demonstrations

parameters.max_branching_factor: up to five evaluation criteria (varied 2 to 5 in Table 10; best agreement at 4)
parameters.merge_for_evaluation: non-neural sum of criterion scores used for all reported results; neural LLM merge also defined
parameters.story_branches: two concept groups and one shared story topic

metrics.name: LLM-Human Agreement (Ag)
metrics.definition: agreement of LLM verdict with human votes, in [0,1], for turn-1, turn-2 and overall

metrics.name: Position Bias (PB)
metrics.definition: fraction of samples where the judgment changes with the encoding order of responses

metrics.name: Length Bias (LB)
metrics.definition: fraction of samples where humans prefer the shorter response but the evaluator does not

metrics.name: All Present (AP)
metrics.definition: fraction of stories with no missing concept

metrics.name: Missing Concepts (MC)
metrics.definition: average percentage of missing concepts; a concept is missing if it appears in no word form

metrics.name: GPT-4 pairwise story preference
metrics.definition: pairwise GPT-4 judgment run twice with order swapped, preferring a story only if both agree

eval.protocol: No significance tests or multiple seeds reported. Agreement uses each human vote independently (Table 9 recomputes with majority vote). Self-enhancement checked only as agreement on the subset where one response comes from GPT-4.

availability.data: MT-Bench public; CommonGen-hard file from the self-refine repository

prompts.text:
Given a set of concepts, we want to write a concise and coherent story consisting of a few sentences using those concepts. In order to do so, you task is to first propose a story topic and then divide the concepts into two groups such that the story generated from each group of concepts can be combined together to form a longer story. Make sure that you do not leave out any concepts.
Concepts: {concepts}

evidence.quote: the non-neural merge of summing up the criterion-wise evaluations is simple and works well in practice

results.claim: BSM with LLaMA-2-70B-chat raises overall human agreement on MT-Bench writing questions from 0.43 (zero-shot relative) to 0.55 and cuts position bias from 51.66 to 17.33.
results.setup: MT-Bench writing, LLaMA-2-70B-chat base, both response orders; baselines relative 0.43, absolute 0.45, Plan&Solve 0.43, Self-Consistency 0.52
results.table: Table 1, row BSM, column Overall Ag (PB 17.33)

results.claim: Authors state BSM improves human agreement by up to an absolute 26% over zero-shot and self-consistency baselines with LLaMA-2-70B-chat.
results.setup: MT-Bench, LLaMA-2-70B-chat, largest gain across domains (STEM: 0.46 to 0.72)
results.quote: BSM with LLaMA-2-70B-chat improves LLM- human agreement by up to absolute 26%
results.note: Quote reflowed from line breaks; STEM row of Table 5 shows 0.72 vs 0.46

results.claim: BSM beats self-consistency at similar compute (0.55 vs 0.52 agreement, PB 17.33 vs 35.66).
results.setup: writing, LLaMA-2-70B-chat; self-consistency samples as many generations as BSM's branching factor, temperature 0.7; value is the self-consistency baseline, BSM is 0.55
results.table: Table 1, row Self-Consistency, column Overall Ag (PB 35.66)

results.claim: BSM improves agreement for every base LLM on writing questions, and GPT-4 gains 3 points (0.59 to 0.62), with no position-bias reduction for GPT-4 (17.33 to 17.00).
results.setup: writing; LLaMA-2-7B 0.39 to 0.41, Vicuna-33B 0.51 to 0.56, LLaMA-2-70B 0.43 to 0.55
results.quote: applying BSM obtains a further improvement of 3%

results.claim: With reference answers, BSM LLaMA-2-70B-chat beats zero-shot on coding, reasoning, math and beats GPT-4 on math (0.64 vs 0.62).
results.setup: MT-Bench Math, GPT-4 generated reference answer fed to solve module; GPT-4 evaluator 0.62
results.table: Table 4, row BSM (w/ LLaMA-2-70B-c), column Math Ag

results.claim: On STEM, BSM LLaMA-2-70B-chat matches GPT-4 agreement (0.72) with lower position bias (10.33 vs 13.66).
results.table: Table 5, Stem, row BSM (w/ LLaMA-2-70B-c), column Overall Ag

results.claim: On the subset where GPT-4 judges its own response, BSM agreement is 0.54 vs 0.51 zero-shot.
results.setup: MT-Bench writing subset where one response is GPT-4's; not a direct measure of self-enhancement bias per the authors
results.table: Table 2, row BSM (w/ GPT-4), column Ag

results.claim: On constrained story generation with LLaMA-2-70B-chat, BSM reaches 28.0 All-Present and 14.7 missing concepts vs zero-shot 22.0 and 27.2.
results.setup: 100 stories of 10 concepts, greedy decoding; LLaMA-2-7B-chat BSM AP 23.0 vs zero-shot 15.0
results.table: Table 6, row BSM, column LLaMA-2-70B-chat AP

results.claim: GPT-4 prefers BSM stories over zero-shot stories 93% of the time.
results.setup: LLaMA-2-70B-chat, order swapped and counted only when consistent
results.quote: stories generated by BSM are preferred a substantial 93% of the time by GPT-4

results.claim: Even BSM with LLaMA-2-70B-chat omits at least one concept in 72% of stories; 60% of the failures arise in the solve module and 12% in merge.
results.quote: omits at least one concept for 72% of the samples

results.claim: Maximum branching factor 4 gives the highest agreement (0.53); position bias keeps falling to 12.00 at BF 5.
results.table: Table 10, row BF 4, column Overall Ag

results.claim: Adding self-consistency inside each branch (BSM+SC, 5 samples, temperature 0.7) leaves agreement at 0.55 and lowers position bias from 17.33 to 15.33.
results.table: Table 8, row BSM + SC, column Overall PB

limits: Authors do not evaluate safety, toxicity or bias of generations.
Length bias is hard to measure in isolation; humans also prefer longer responses.
Recursive or multi-level BSM is not explored because of cost.
Efficiency gains from parallel decomposition are not measured; no token or latency cost is reported, although BSM makes many more LLM calls (branch + k solves + merge, twice per item) than zero-shot.
BSM does not reduce position bias for GPT-4 (17.33 to 17.00 only) and the GPT-4 agreement gain is 3 points on one category; no significance tests, single greedy run, no seeds.
Self-enhancement bias is only approximated by agreement on a subset.
Constrained generation uses only 100 samples and two LLaMA-2 models; scale gives little help and 72% of BSM stories still miss a concept.
Reference-based evaluation depends on GPT-4 reference answers being curated once.
Models studied (LLaMA-2, Vicuna, GPT-4 of 2023) have dated.
